case_title: Prosecutor v. Bosco Ntaganda — rape and sexual slavery within the same armed group
question: Can members of an armed group be victims of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute when the crimes are committed against them by members of the same armed group?
facts: The accused was charged with crimes committed during a non-international armed conflict in Ituri, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by the Union des Patriotes Congolais/Forces Patriotiques pour la Libération du Congo (UPC/FPLC). Two counts charged the rape and the sexual slavery of UPC/FPLC child soldiers, as war crimes under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute; the alleged victims were members of the UPC/FPLC and the alleged perpetrators were also members of the UPC/FPLC. The defence challenged the Court's jurisdiction over these counts, arguing that under the established framework of international law, members of an armed group are not protected against crimes committed by their own group, and that a member of an armed force attains protection only on ceasing to be a member, laying down arms or being placed hors de combat. A Trial Chamber held that the Court had jurisdiction, and the defence appealed.
holding: In its Judgment of 15 June 2017, the ICC Appeals Chamber unanimously confirmed the Trial Chamber's decision that the Court has jurisdiction over the two counts. Members of an armed force or group are not categorically excluded from protection against the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(b)(xxii) and (e)(vi); there are no requirements that victims be protected persons in the sense of the grave breaches provisions or persons taking no active part in hostilities under Common Article 3. It is the nexus requirement, that the conduct took place in the context of and was associated with an armed conflict, that delineates war crimes from ordinary crimes.
confidence_reasoning: The Rome Statute text is clear and the arguments are well-grounded in its provisions. The only reason confidence is not higher is that the Appeals Chamber's reasoning in the actual case (Ntaganda) is not in the retrieved context, so I rely solely on statutory interpretation. No objections were raised to test the arguments.

verdict.conclusion: Yes. Members of an armed group can be victims of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute when the crimes are committed against them by members of the same armed group. The provision does not limit victim status to civilians; it criminalizes the enumerated acts of sexual violence as serious violations of Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions. Article 8(2)(c) expressly defines protected persons to include "members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention or any other cause." Child soldiers under fifteen are entitled to this protection irrespective of formal membership. The Trial Chamber correctly exercised jurisdiction.
verdict.reasoning: All three arguments survive unchallenged because no objections were filed. Argument arg_b6c3d313 correctly notes that Article 8(2)(e)(vi) lists the prohibited acts without qualifying the victim as a civilian and incorporates violations of Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions. Argument arg_f8b6ec69 demonstrates that Article 8(2)(c) extends protection to members of armed forces who are hors de combat, and this definition applies to Article 8(2)(e)(vi) because the sexual violence there is described as a violation of Article 3. Argument arg_7ec68acb adds that child soldiers under fifteen are protected as persons not taking active part in hostilities. The defence's jurisdictional challenge — that members of an armed group are never protected against their own group — is inconsistent with the text of Articles 8(2)(c) and (e)(vi), which protect persons hors de combat regardless of affiliation.

arguments.claim: Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute criminalises rape and sexual slavery in a non‑international armed conflict regardless of whether the victim is a civilian or a member of the same armed group.
arguments.reasoning: The provision lists the prohibited acts in its own terms and does not qualify the victim as a civilian. By expressly including "any other form of sexual violence also constituting a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions" it captures violations committed against any protected person, which includes members of armed groups who are hors de combat. Therefore the alleged victims, although members of UPC/FPLC, fall within the scope of the war‑crime definition.
